table.text: Only participants in the first three generations actually made decisions, and the next generation was recruited only if the previous generation had passed the pool on; after the third generation had made its decisions, its contributions determined whether the pool would be passed on to the fourth generation, for which no participants were recruited.

A total of 183 participants were included in the anonymous and future-generation decision disclosure (hereafter, future-generation disclosure) conditions: 75 in the anonymous condition (69 women; Mage = 20.27 years, SD = 1.48) and 108 in the futuregeneration disclosure condition (94 women; Mage = 20.10 years, SD = 1.18).
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of psychiatric disorders.

Following the classification criteria of Murphy et al. (2011), participants with SVO angles ≥ 22.45° were classified as prosocial and those with angles < 22.45° as proself; in this experiment, two participants were competitive (< -12.04°) and were included in the proself category.

table.text: The difference was that, in the peer disclosure and name-and-face disclosure conditions, participants were told that their decisions and related information would be disclosed to the other two members of their group.

Before making their contribution decisions, participants were told that, after this round of contributions, their contribution, name, and photograph would be disclosed to the other two group members and that they would also see the other two members' results; they were then shown an example of the disclosure screen, which displayed two faces (Faces 2 and 4), with the names and contributions replaced by the placeholders "Zhang San" and "Li Si" and "X" and "Y," respectively.

Because future-generation and peer disclosure were tested against a shared anonymous baseline, the contrast between them is indirect, and the two audiences differed in more than their presence at the time of decision: peers were co-actors who faced the same choice, whose own contributions were also disclosed, and with whom participants might have expected further contact, whereas the next generation consisted of recipients whom participants had no reason to expect to meet.

A second limitation concerns the sample: given the constraints, participants were recruited in two waves and had an uneven age and gender composition, and a broader sample is needed to test the boundaries of these conclusions.

Participants in the anonymous and peer disclosure conditions were recruited in spring 2024 in the same recruitment wave as those in the futuregeneration disclosure condition of Experiment 1, whereas participants in the name-and-face disclosure condition were recruited separately in November 2024 (data collection ended on November 27).

Participants in the anonymous and peer disclosure conditions were recruited in spring 2024 in the same recruitment wave as those in the future-generation disclosure condition of Experiment 1; participants in the name-and-face disclosure condition were recruited separately in November 2024 (see Section 3.1.1).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Following Lohse and Waichman (2020), each generational sequence comprised four generations, and each condition started with 18 first-generation groups. Only participants in the first three generations actually made decisions, and the next generation was recruited only if the previous generation had passed the pool on; after the third generation had made its decisions, its contributions determined whether the pool would be passed on to the fourth generation, for which no participants were recruited. A total of 183 participants were included in the anonymous and future-generation decision disclosure (hereafter, future-generation disclosure) conditions: 75 in the anonymous condition (69 women; Mage = 20.27 years, SD = 1.48) and 108 in the futuregeneration disclosure condition (94 women; Mage = 20.10 years, SD = 1.18). Because the total sample size depended on how many pools were passed on and could not be fixed in advance, we conducted a sensitivity power analysis instead of an a priori power analysis in G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007 (Faul et al.,, 2009; ANOVA: Fixed effects, special, main effects and interactions). With α = .05, a total sample size of N = 183, four groups, and a numerator df of 1, the design had 80% power to detect effects of at least f = 0.21 (approximately ηp² = .04) for the main effect of disclosure condition and its interaction with SVO; with 90% and 95% power, the minimum detectable effects were f = 0.24 and 0.27, respectively. Because cell sizes were unequal, these values are approximate. All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of psychiatric disorders. They signed an informed consent form before the experiment and were paid after it. The study was approved by the local ethics committee. Data were collected in spring 2024.

A sensitivity power analysis was again conducted in G*Power 3.1 (ANOVA:

Participants in Experiment 2 were recruited and selected in the same way as in Experiment 1. The first generation again consisted of 18 groups, and the next generation was recruited only if the previous generation had passed the pool on; three generations were actually run. In total, 354 participants were included in the anonymous, peer decision disclosure (hereafter, peer disclosure), and peer name-and-face disclosure (hereafter, name-and-face disclosure) conditions: 75 in the anonymous condition (69 women; Mage = 20.27 years, SD = 1.48; these participants were drawn from Experiment 1), 132 in the peer disclosure condition Fixed effects, special, main effects and interactions). With α = .05, a total sample size of N = 354, six groups, and a numerator df of 2, the design had 80% power to detect effects of at least f = 0.17 (approximately ηp² = .03), which can serve as an approximate reference for the three-level main effect and its interaction with the other factor; with 90% and 95% power, the minimum detectable effects were approximately f = 0.19 and 0.21, respectively. Because cell sizes were unequal, these values are approximate. Because of the different recruitment waves, participants in the name-and-face disclosure condition were older than those in the other two conditions, F(2, 350) = 103.19, p < .001, ηp² = .371. The proportion of women also differed across the three conditions (92.0%, 83.3%, and 70.1%, respectively), χ 2 (2, N = 354) = 16.50, p < .001, V = .22.

table.text: Participants in the future-generation disclosure condition perceived a significantly greater impact on their reputation (M = 5.96, SD = 2.15) than those in the anonymous condition (M = 3.63, SD = 1.85), t(172.84) = 7.85, p < .001, d = 1.15, 95% CI [0.83, 1.46], indicating that the reputation manipulation was successful.

table.text: The proportion of prosocial individuals did not differ significantly between the anonymous (52.0%) and future-generation disclosure (63.0%) conditions, χ 2 (1, N = 183) = 2.19, p = .139, V = .11, nor did SVO angles, F(1, 181) = 2.69, p = .103, ηp² = .015, 90% CI [.000,.056].

The main effect of SVO was significant, F(1, 179) = 31.28, p < .001, ηp² = .149, 90% CI [.076, .227]: Prosocial individuals (EMM = 5.28, SE = 0.16) contributed significantly more than proself individuals (EMM = 3.96, SE = 0.18).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. #### README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including 'README' in the name of your overview document.
#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 73 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (72), R history (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 195 columns across 20 data files.
#### Careless Responding

1 distinct respondent was flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **1 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Respondent = "95", "Blocks flagged" = 1L, Scales = "q (1-9, 6 items)", 
    "Longest run" = "same answer 6 times in a row, out of 6 items (flagged at 5)", 
    "Short-scale only" = "yes"), row.names = 1L, class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE)
```

**What this does not cover.** Only 2 of 20 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

ethics_statements: The study was approved by the local ethics committee.
Informed consent, payment, and ethics approval were the same as in Experiment 1.
live_data_statements: In Experiment 1, disclosing to the next generation what participants had contributed increased the rate of sustained generations but did not reliably increase individual contributions or narrow the gap between prosocial and proself individuals.

In the future-generation decision disclosure condition, following previous manipulations of reputational cues (Arfer et al., 2015), participants were told before making their contribution decisions that their decisions would be disclosed to >Method

Only participants in the first three generations actually made decisions, and the next generation was recruited only if the previous generation had passed the pool on; after the third generation had made its decisions, its contributions determined whether the pool would be passed on to the fourth generation, for which no participants were recruited.

A total of 183 participants were included in the anonymous and future-generation decision disclosure (hereafter, future-generation disclosure) conditions: 75 in the anonymous condition (69 women; Mage = 20.27 years, SD = 1.48) and 108 in the futuregeneration disclosure condition (94 women; Mage = 20.10 years, SD = 1.18).
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of psychiatric disorders.

Following the classification criteria of Murphy et al. (2011), participants with SVO angles ≥ 22.45° were classified as prosocial and those with angles < 22.45° as proself; in this experiment, two participants were competitive (< -12.04°) and were included in the proself category.

The task was presented as a generational sequence: Participants were told that each sequence involved 12 participants randomly assigned to four three-person groups, that each group represented one generation, and that the generations would make their decisions one after another.
Participants were told that the tokens they kept would be converted into payment at a fixed rate.

Unlike Lohse and Waichman (2020), who informed participants of their position in the generational sequence, we did not reveal to participants which generation they were in; instead, all participants were told that their group was neither the first nor the last.

In addition, all participants were told that their final earnings depended on the decisions of the previous group and on their own decisions, and that their own decisions would also affect the earnings of the next group.
Before the task, participants were explicitly told that their individual contributions would be kept completely confidential.

Before the task, participants were likewise explicitly told that their individual contributions, together with those of the other two members, would be shown to the three members of the next generation.
Participants in Experiment 2 were recruited and selected in the same way as in Experiment 1.

In total, 354 participants were included in the anonymous, peer decision disclosure (hereafter, peer disclosure), and peer name-and-face disclosure (hereafter, name-and-face disclosure) conditions: 75 in the anonymous condition (69 women; Mage = 20.27 years, SD = 1.48; these participants were drawn from Experiment 1), 132 in the peer disclosure condition Fixed effects, special, main effects and interactions).
Age data for one participant were treated as missing because of an entry error, so age statistics are based on 353 participants.

The face stimuli were prepared following the general procedure of Gong et al. (2011): Eight undergraduates (four men and four women) were recruited from a university, and photographs of their neutral facial expressions were taken under standardized conditions.

The difference was that, in the peer disclosure and name-and-face disclosure conditions, participants were told that their decisions and related information would be disclosed to the other two members of their group.

Before making their contribution decisions, participants were told that, after this round of contributions, their contribution, name, and photograph would be disclosed to the other two group members and that they would also see the other two members' results; they were then shown an example of the disclosure screen, which displayed two faces (Faces 2 and 4), with the names and contributions replaced by the placeholders "Zhang San" and "Li Si" and "X" and "Y," respectively.

Because future-generation and peer disclosure were tested against a shared anonymous baseline, the contrast between them is indirect, and the two audiences differed in more than their presence at the time of decision: peers were co-actors who faced the same choice, whose own contributions were also disclosed, and with whom participants might have expected further contact, whereas the next generation consisted of recipients whom participants had no reason to expect to meet.

A second limitation concerns the sample: given the constraints, participants were recruited in two waves and had an uneven age and gender composition, and a broader sample is needed to test the boundaries of these conclusions.

Participants in the anonymous and peer disclosure conditions were recruited in spring 2024 in the same recruitment wave as those in the futuregeneration disclosure condition of Experiment 1, whereas participants in the name-and-face disclosure condition were recruited separately in November 2024 (data collection ended on November 27).

Participants in the anonymous and peer disclosure conditions were recruited in spring 2024 in the same recruitment wave as those in the future-generation disclosure condition of Experiment 1; participants in the name-and-face disclosure condition were recruited separately in November 2024 (see Section 3.1.1).

**1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: `Final_E2.csv` to `data/Final_E2.csv` (in 00_import_and_cleaning.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file.

#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 5 scripts: 4 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 1 was run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **3 scripts stopped on a file another script writes**, so they were run once more after the other scripts: `02_experiment2.R` (Final_E2.csv); `03_supplementary_analyses.R` (Final_E2.csv); `run_all.R` (Final_E2.csv). Then these ran to the end: `02_experiment2.R`, `03_supplementary_analyses.R`, `run_all.R`. Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_). **A script looked for a file in another folder than the deposit has it**, so before running it once more we copied it there: `data_and_analysis_code.zip/data_and_analysis_code/data/Final_E2.csv` to `data_and_analysis_code.zip/data_and_analysis_code/data/data/Final_E2.csv` for `01_experiment1.R`. Building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.

), Outcome = c("run_by_source", "ran_ok", "ran_ok", "ran_ok", 
"ran_ok"), Detail = c("", "", "", "", ""), "Time (s)" = c(0, 
3.7, 4, 3.8, 4.7)), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)

**Calls that install packages in the code**

1 call to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like was replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.
**Run by another script**

1 script is run by another script with `source()`, so it was not run on its own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on its own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Its outcome is part of the sourcing script's outcome.

text.text: Many environmental problems, from climate change to resource depletion, are intergenerational dilemmas: the present generation bears conservation costs, whereas the benefits go to future generations, who can neither observe nor reciprocate.
Reputation reliably sustains cooperation among contemporaries, but whether it works across generations remains unclear.

In two experiments using an intergenerational goods game, we examined how the audience of disclosure and the type of information disclosed affect contributions to a resource passed from one generation to the next, and whether social value orientation (SVO) moderates these effects.

In Experiment 1, disclosing to the next generation what participants had contributed increased the rate of sustained generations but did not reliably increase individual contributions or narrow the gap between prosocial and proself individuals.
In Experiment 2, disclosing the same information to present peers increased both individual contributions and the rate of sustained generations.
Adding names and faces was tentatively associated with a further increase in contributions, although this condition was recruited in a separate wave.
These gains came mainly from proself individuals, whose contributions no longer differed significantly from those of prosocial individuals when names and faces were disclosed.

Findings suggest that disclosure promotes intergenerational cooperation chiefly when it reaches an audience present at the time of decision, and that disclosure, especially identifiable disclosure, matters most for those least motivated to cooperate.
Making conservation visible to future generations may not be enough; it may also need to be visible to someone now, suggesting a potentially low-cost approach to promoting environmental cooperation.
Humanity is currently facing a series of severe global challenges, including climate change, biodiversity loss, and resource depletion (United Nations Environment Programme [UNEP], 2025).

These problems pose a serious threat to ecological stability and human wellbeing, and addressing them requires sustained intergenerational cooperation, in which the present generation forgoes immediate benefits to conserve resources for future generations.

Unlike cooperation among contemporaries, intergenerational cooperation is temporally asymmetric: The present generation bears the costs, whereas future generations reap the benefits, creating an inherent conflict of interest between present decision makers and future stakeholders (Wade-Benzoni & Tost, 2009).
text.formatted: Unlike cooperation among contemporaries, intergenerational cooperation is temporally asymmetric: The present generation bears the costs, whereas future generations reap the benefits, creating an inherent conflict of interest between present decision makers and future stakeholders <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Wade-Benzoni & Tost, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, because people today cannot directly experience the needs of future generations and need not worry about being held accountable by them, cooperation with the future is fragile: Even when most people conserve, a self-interested minority can be enough to deplete a shared resource (Hauser et al., 2014; Lohse & Waichman, 2020), especially when earlier generations have already acted unsustainably (Shahen et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Moreover, because people today cannot directly experience the needs of future generations and need not worry about being held accountable by them, cooperation with the future is fragile: Even when most people conserve, a self-interested minority can be enough to deplete a shared resource <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Hauser et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Lohse & Waichman, 2020)</ref>, especially when earlier generations have already acted unsustainably <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Shahen et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: How, then, can intergenerational cooperation be promoted?
A Chinese saying holds that a good name lasts for a hundred generations, suggesting that reputation may reach across generations.

Research on cooperation among contemporaries has shown that reputation can sustain cooperation when individuals' decisions are visible to others who can later respond to them: people preferentially help those who have been generous in the past (Wedekind & Milinski, 2000), and the need to maintain such a reputation keeps contributions to a public good high, whereas contributions drop quickly once no further opportunities for reciprocation are expected (Milinski et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Research on cooperation among contemporaries has shown that reputation can sustain cooperation when individuals' decisions are visible to others who can later respond to them: people preferentially help those who have been generous in the past <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Wedekind & Milinski, 2000)</ref>, and the need to maintain such a reputation keeps contributions to a public good high, whereas contributions drop quickly once no further opportunities for reciprocation are expected <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Milinski et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, previous studies suggest that people are willing to make sacrifices for future generations partly because they wish to leave a positive legacy and to be remembered favorably (Wade-Benzoni & Tost, 2009; Zaval et al., 2015).
text.formatted: In addition, previous studies suggest that people are willing to make sacrifices for future generations partly because they wish to leave a positive legacy and to be remembered favorably <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Wade-Benzoni & Tost, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Zaval et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Because legacy concerns are about how one will be seen by others, they can be regarded as a form of reputational concern that extends across generations.
A key question in intergenerational dilemmas is to whom reputational information should be disclosed for it to constrain behavior.
The most obvious candidate audience is future generations.

Because future generations ultimately inherit the outcomes of intergenerational cooperation, they are the evaluators with the greatest stake in the present generation's behavior, and people do care about how they will be remembered by future generations (Mah et al., 2024; Wade-Benzoni, 2019; Zaval et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Because future generations ultimately inherit the outcomes of intergenerational cooperation, they are the evaluators with the greatest stake in the present generation's behavior, and people do care about how they will be remembered by future generations <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Mah et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Wade-Benzoni, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Zaval et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, future generations are an absent audience: They cannot observe individuals' decisions as they are made, nor can they respond in real time.
Experiment 1 tested whether such an audience can still exert enough reputational pressure to promote intergenerational cooperation.
Apart from future generations, members of one's own generation are another natural reputational audience.

Previous research has shown that when individuals realize that their behavior will be observed and evaluated by their contemporaries, they often adjust their decisions to maintain a good reputation (Milinski et al., 2002; Wedekind & Milinski, 2000), and some even cooperate without checking the costs in order to appear trustworthy (Jordan et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Previous research has shown that when individuals realize that their behavior will be observed and evaluated by their contemporaries, they often adjust their decisions to maintain a good reputation <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Milinski et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Wedekind & Milinski, 2000)</ref>, and some even cooperate without checking the costs in order to appear trustworthy <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Jordan et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Compared with future generations, members of the same generation are real observers who are present when decisions are made and can observe and evaluate them immediately; in theory, this presence may make reputational pressure more effective.

Yet no study has directly tested whether disclosing decisions to peers can promote intergenerational cooperation, and whether it might even do so more effectively than disclosure to future generations.
Experiment 2 tested this possibility and then asked whether the effect could be strengthened.
Beyond the audience, individuals' reputational concern may also depend on how much of their identity information is disclosed.

Reputational information can include more than the behavior itself: how observable an act is depends both on what is revealed about the actor's behavior and on what is revealed about the actor's identity, such as their name and facial photograph (Bradley et al., 2018). Christens et al. (2019) found that, compared with an anonymous condition, revealing the identities of individual decision makers increased their contributions in a public goods game, an effect the authors attributed to individuals' sensitivity to others' opinions; Sampaio et al. (2023) further showed that information about co-players' identities affected participants' cooperation only when it was presented together with information about those co-players' past behavior.

(2019)</ref> found that, compared with an anonymous condition, revealing the identities of individual decision makers increased their contributions in a public goods game, an effect the authors attributed to individuals' sensitivity to others' opinions; <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Sampaio et al. (2023)</ref> further showed that information about co-players' identities affected participants' cooperation only when it was presented together with information about those co-players' past behavior.

text.text: Building on these findings, Experiment 2 also tested whether intergenerational cooperation would receive an additional boost when the type of information disclosed was expanded (from disclosing decisions only to disclosing both decisions and identity information).
However, individuals may respond differently to the same reputational cues.

Social value orientation (SVO), a relatively stable personality trait, distinguishes prosocial individuals, who care more about collective welfare, from proself individuals, who care more about their own interests (Murphy et al., 2011; Pletzer et al., 2018; Van Lange et al., 1997).
text.formatted: Social value orientation (SVO), a relatively stable personality trait, distinguishes prosocial individuals, who care more about collective welfare, from proself individuals, who care more about their own interests <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Murphy et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Pletzer et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Van Lange et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Research on prosocial behavior among contemporaries has found that egoistic (proself) individuals behave generously mainly when their behavior is public and can therefore be reciprocated by others, whereas altruistic (prosocial) individuals behave generously regardless of whether such reputational incentives are present (Simpson & Willer, 2008).
text.formatted: Research on prosocial behavior among contemporaries has found that egoistic (proself) individuals behave generously mainly when their behavior is public and can therefore be reciprocated by others, whereas altruistic (prosocial) individuals behave generously regardless of whether such reputational incentives are present <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Simpson & Willer, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: One explanation lies in the different sources of cooperative motivation in the two types of individuals: Prosocial individuals' cooperation is driven more by relatively stable intrinsic motives, so they are more likely to cooperate voluntarily even without external pressure; proself individuals, in contrast, rely more on weighing the external costs and benefits of the situation, so their decisions tend to be more sensitive to external signals (Simpson & Willer, 2008; Sun & Ling, 2023; Van Lange et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2016).
text.formatted: One explanation lies in the different sources of cooperative motivation in the two types of individuals: Prosocial individuals' cooperation is driven more by relatively stable intrinsic motives, so they are more likely to cooperate voluntarily even without external pressure; proself individuals, in contrast, rely more on weighing the external costs and benefits of the situation, so their decisions tend to be more sensitive to external signals <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Simpson & Willer, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Sun & Ling, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Van Lange et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Wu et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore measured SVO and examined whether proself individuals would adjust their behavior in response to changes in reputational cues and thereby come closer to prosocial individuals in intergenerational cooperation.

text.text: Experiment 1 used the IGG paradigm with two conditions: an anonymous condition and a future-generation decision disclosure condition.
In the anonymous condition, participants' token contributions were kept completely confidential.

In the future-generation decision disclosure condition, following previous manipulations of reputational cues (Arfer et al., 2015), participants were told before making their contribution decisions that their decisions would be disclosed to  >Method
text.formatted: In the future-generation decision disclosure condition, following previous manipulations of reputational cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Arfer et al., 2015)</ref>, participants were told before making their contribution decisions that their decisions would be disclosed to <head n="2.1." >Method</head>

text.text: Following Lohse and Waichman (2020), each generational sequence comprised four generations, and each condition started with 18 first-generation groups.

Only participants in the first three generations actually made decisions, and the next generation was recruited only if the previous generation had passed the pool on; after the third generation had made its decisions, its contributions determined whether the pool would be passed on to the fourth generation, for which no participants were recruited.

A total of 183 participants were included in the anonymous and future-generation decision disclosure (hereafter, future-generation disclosure) conditions: 75 in the anonymous condition (69 women; Mage = 20.27 years, SD = 1.48) and 108 in the futuregeneration disclosure condition (94 women; Mage = 20.10 years, SD = 1.18).

Because the total sample size depended on how many pools were passed on and could not be fixed in advance, we conducted a sensitivity power analysis instead of an a priori power analysis in G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007 (Faul et al., , 2009; ANOVA: Fixed effects, special, main effects and interactions).

text.text: With α = .05, a total sample size of N = 183, four groups, and a numerator df of 1, the design had 80% power to detect effects of at least f = 0.21 (approximately ηp² = .04) for the main effect of disclosure condition and its interaction with SVO; with 90% and 95% power, the minimum detectable effects were f = 0.24 and 0.27, respectively.
Because cell sizes were unequal, these values are approximate.
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of psychiatric disorders.
They signed an informed consent form before the experiment and were paid after it.
The study was approved by the local ethics committee.
Data were collected in spring 2024.
Social Value Orientation.
SVO was measured with the six primary items of the SVO Slider Measure developed by Murphy et al. (2011), each of which offers nine options for allocating money between oneself and another person.
text.formatted: SVO was measured with the six primary items of the SVO Slider Measure developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Murphy et al. (2011)</ref>, each of which offers nine options for allocating money between oneself and another person.

text.text: The SVO angle was computed as SVO° = arctan [(Āo -50)/(Ās -50)], where Āo and Ās are the mean allocations to the other and to the self, respectively, across the six items.

Following the classification criteria of Murphy et al. (2011), participants with SVO angles ≥ 22.45° were classified as prosocial and those with angles < 22.45° as proself; in this experiment, two participants were competitive (< -12.04°) and were included in the proself category.

text.text: After making their contribution decisions, participants answered the question "In the situation you just experienced, how much do you think your reputation will be affected?"
on a 9-point scale (1 = not affected at all,9 = extremely affected).
We used the IGG as adapted by Lohse and Waichman (2020).
text.formatted: We used the IGG as adapted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Lohse and Waichman (2020)</ref>.

text.text: The task was presented as a generational sequence: Participants were told that each sequence involved 12 participants randomly assigned to four three-person groups, that each group represented one generation, and that the generations would make their decisions one after another.
Each participant was endowed with 10 tokens and decided how many of them (0-10) to contribute to a common resource pool.

If the total contribution of the three group members reached the contribution threshold (≥ 15 tokens), the pool was replenished to its initial level and passed on to the next generation, whose three members likewise each received 10 tokens and made their decisions; if the total fell short of 15 tokens, the sequence ended immediately and all later generations received nothing.
Participants were told that the tokens they kept would be converted into payment at a fixed rate.

Unlike Lohse and Waichman (2020), who informed participants of their position in the generational sequence, we did not reveal to participants which generation they were in; instead, all participants were told that their group was neither the first nor the last.
text.formatted: Unlike <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Lohse and Waichman (2020)</ref>, who informed participants of their position in the generational sequence, we did not reveal to participants which generation they were in; instead, all participants were told that their group was neither the first nor the last.

text.text: This was intended to place all participants in the same psychological position: Participants at the start of a sequence have no preceding generation from which to inherit the pool, and those at the end have no subsequent generation to pass it on to, so the decision situations they face differ substantially from those of the middle generations.
With this adjustment, every participant was, by design, both a recipient and a transmitter of the resource.
Three generations were actually run, and the contributions of the third generation determined whether the sequence would continue to the fourth generation.

(B) The pool is not passed on.

At the beginning of the experiment, the experimenter explained the rules of the IGG in detail and told participants that they would complete the task together with two other participants whom they did not know.

Before the formal task, participants answered comprehension questions to confirm that they fully understood the task; if they answered incorrectly, the experimenter explained the rules again until they passed the comprehension check.

In addition, all participants were told that their final earnings depended on the decisions of the previous group and on their own decisions, and that their own decisions would also affect the earnings of the next group.
In the IGG, participants first made their contribution decisions and completed the reputation manipulation check.
They then saw a waiting screen with the message "Collecting the results of the other group members.
Please wait…" After the wait, participants received feedback, and the information they saw differed depending on the disclosure condition.
There were two disclosure conditions in this experiment.
In the anonymous condition, participants saw only their group's total contribution and whether the pool would be passed on to the next generation; no member's individual contribution was shown.
Before the task, participants were explicitly told that their individual contributions would be kept completely confidential.
In the future-generation disclosure condition, participants saw, in addition to the information above, their own contribution and the contribution of each of the other two group members.

Before the task, participants were likewise explicitly told that their individual contributions, together with those of the other two members, would be shown to the three members of the next generation.
Participants then completed the SVO measure.
Statistical analyses were conducted in R using the car and emmeans packages.
All tests were two-tailed, with α = .05.

Because cell sizes were unequal, analyses of variance (ANOVAs) used Type III sums of squares with effect coding; marginal means for main effects are reported as estimated marginal means (EMMs) with their standard errors (SEs).
For F tests, we report partial eta squared (ηp² ) with its 90% confidence interval (CI ; Steiger, 2004).

Cohen's d was computed as the difference between EMMs divided by the square root of the mean squared error (√MSE); in this experiment, MSE = 2.40.
The reputation manipulation check was analyzed with Welch's t test (Delacre et al., 2017), and d was computed using the pooled standard deviation.

Following previous research (Hauser et al., 2014; Lohse & Waichman, 2020), we also computed two indices of sustained generations at the group level.

text.text: With the three-person group as the unit of analysis, a group was counted as having passed the pool on to the next generation when its members' total contribution reached the contribution threshold (≥ 15 tokens) and as having failed otherwise.

Aggregating across generations, the rate of sustained generations was the proportion of all potential future generations (Generations 2-4 of each generational sequence; 54 per condition) that were sustained, and the conditional rate of sustained generations was the proportion of groups that passed the pool on among all groups that made decisions, which corresponds to the conditional likelihood reported by Lohse and Waichman (2020).

text.text: To examine whether disclosure to future generations increased the rate of sustained generations at the group level, we conducted chi-square tests on both indices.

The rate of sustained generations was significantly higher in the future-generation disclosure condition (42.6%, 23 of 54 potential future generations) than in the anonymous condition (14.8%, 8 of 54), χ 2 (1, N = 108) = 10.18, p = .001, V = .31.

The rate of sustained generations in the anonymous condition (14.8%) closely matched the no-punishment baseline reported by Lohse and Waichman (2020; 14%), suggesting that our adaptation reproduces the baseline of the laboratory IGG.
In addition, to examine the effect of future-generation disclosure over a longer time horizon, we ran bootstrapping simulations on the observed decisions, following Hauser et al. (2014).

text.text: Specifically, we simulated 10,000 pools for each condition.

In each generation, the contributions of the three members were randomly sampled, with replacement, from the decisions of all participants in that condition; if the total contribution of that generation reached the contribution threshold (≥ 15 tokens), the pool was sustained and passed on to the next generation, and otherwise the pool was depleted and the simulation ended.
Each simulation ran for up to 15 generations, and we recorded the proportion of pools sustained in each generation (see Figure 3).

text.text: In the anonymous condition, pools were depleted rapidly: Only 16.4% of the pools were still sustained after two generations, falling to 1.0% after five generations, and almost all pools were depleted after nine generations.
In the future-generation disclosure condition, pools were sustained considerably longer: 43.6% after two generations and 12.0% after five generations, with 0.2% still sustained after 15 generations.

It should be noted that this simulation was extrapolated from the observed data and involved no statistical tests; the differences between conditions reflect only the overall trends shown by the simulation.

Experiment 1 examined whether disclosing the decisions of members of the current generation to future generations promotes intergenerational cooperation.

At the individual level, the number of tokens that participants contributed to the pool did not differ significantly between the future-generation disclosure and anonymous conditions, and future-generation disclosure did not narrow the gap in contributions between prosocial and proself individuals.

At the group level, both indices of sustained generations were higher in the future-generation disclosure condition than in the anonymous condition, suggesting that future-generation disclosure improved the sustainability of intergenerational resources at the group level.
Taken together, disclosure to future generations did promote intergenerational cooperation to some extent, but the effect was limited.
The two measures yielded different results because of the way the rate of sustained generations is determined.
This measure is based on whether a group's total contribution reaches the contribution threshold, which makes it a binary measure with the threshold as its cutoff.

In both conditions of this experiment, participants' mean contributions were slightly below the fair share of 5 tokens per person, so groups' total contributions were generally close to the threshold (13.40 tokens in the anonymous condition and 14.92 tokens in the future-generation disclosure condition).

When most groups' totals hover around the threshold, small and nonsignificant increases in individual contributions, once summed at the group level, can be enough to push some groups that would otherwise have fallen just short over the threshold, producing an observable difference in the group-level measure.

The results at the two levels are therefore not contradictory; rather, they are consistent with a small effect of future-generation disclosure that was not strong enough to show up reliably in individuals' contribution decisions.
This limited effect may be related to the audience's distance in time.

The constraining effect of reputation on behavior depends on the audience being able to observe individuals' decisions and to evaluate and respond to them accordingly (Milinski et al., 2002; Wedekind & Milinski, 2000).
text.formatted: The constraining effect of reputation on behavior depends on the audience being able to observe individuals' decisions and to evaluate and respond to them accordingly <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Milinski et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Wedekind & Milinski, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Future generations, however, live long after present decision makers and can neither observe their decisions as they happen nor respond to them.

The absence of the audience may have weakened the reputational pressure that disclosure could exert: Although futuregeneration disclosure significantly increased participants' ratings of how much their reputation would be affected (d = 1.15), this perception did not translate into a significant increase in individual contributions.
Experiment 2 therefore turned to another potential audience, peers who are present when decisions are made, to examine whether disclosing decisions to them promotes intergenerational cooperation.

Because disclosing decisions alone conveys behavioral information while leaving the actor unidentified (Bradley et al., 2018), Experiment 2 also tested whether adding names and faces was associated with a further increase.
text.formatted: Because disclosing decisions alone conveys behavioral information while leaving the actor unidentified <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bradley et al., 2018)</ref>, Experiment 2 also tested whether adding names and faces was associated with a further increase.

text.text: Experiment 2 used the same IGG paradigm as Experiment 1 but changed the audience from future generations to present peers and included three conditions.

Specifically, in the anonymous condition, participants' token contributions were kept completely confidential (as in the anonymous condition of Experiment 1); in the peer decision disclosure condition, participants' contributions were shown to the other members of their generation; and in the peer name-and-face disclosure condition, participants' names and faces were shown to the other members of their generation along with their contributions.

This experiment thus tested whether, compared with anonymity, disclosing decisions to present peers increases intergenerational cooperation and whether additionally disclosing names and faces brings a further increase.

Experiment 2 also compared the intergenerational cooperation of prosocial and proself individuals across the three conditions to examine whether, as more information is disclosed, the cooperation of proself individuals approaches that of prosocial individuals and the gap between them narrows accordingly.

The first generation again consisted of 18 groups, and the next generation was recruited only if the previous generation had passed the pool on; three generations were actually run.

text.text: We therefore repeated the analyses with gender (Model 1) and both gender and age (Model 2) as covariates.

Crucially, in both models, all main effects and the Disclosure Condition × SVO interaction remained significant, and the pattern of simple effects and interaction contrasts was largely unchanged when controlling for age and gender.

The only exception was the difference between the name-and-face and peer disclosure conditions, which was not significant after Bonferroni correction in either model (Model 1: p = .067; Model 2: Mdiff = 0.25, p = .802).

Importantly, because age was almost completely confounded with the name-and-face disclosure condition, covariate adjustment cannot fully separate their effects (Miller & Chapman, 2001), and this specific comparison should therefore be interpreted with caution.

Four of the faces (two male and two female) were selected: Faces 2 and 4 were used in the example disclosure screen shown before the decision, and Faces 3 and 5 were used in the feedback screen shown after the decision.

The two faces used in the predecision example were rated below the scale midpoint (4) on attractiveness and arousal and did not differ significantly from the midpoint on trustworthiness, whereas the two faces used in the postdecision feedback were rated above the midpoint on trustworthiness.
For the name stimuli, two common Chinese names (Ding Wenrui and Huang Xinqian) were selected on the basis of expert ratings.
The procedure was largely the same as in Experiment 1.

The difference was that, in the peer disclosure and name-and-face disclosure conditions, participants were told that their decisions and related information would be disclosed to the other two members of their group.
Specifically, in the name-and-face disclosure condition, participants entered their names at the start of the experiment and had a photograph of their face taken and uploaded on site.

Before making their contribution decisions, participants were told that, after this round of contributions, their contribution, name, and photograph would be disclosed to the other two group members and that they would also see the other two members' results; they were then shown an example of the disclosure screen, which displayed two faces (Faces 2 and 4), with the names and contributions replaced by the placeholders "Zhang San" and "Li Si" and "X" and "Y," respectively.

After making their contribution decisions and completing the reputation manipulation check, participants saw the names (Ding Wenrui and Huang Xinqian), faces (Faces 3 and 5), and token contributions of the other two members, and then completed the SVO measure.
Data were analyzed in the same way as in Experiment 1; in this experiment, MSE = 2.20.

Experiment 2 examined whether disclosing individuals' decisions promotes intergenerational cooperation when the audience consists of present peers, and whether additionally disclosing identity information such as names and faces strengthens this effect.

The results showed that, at the individual level, contributions in both the peer disclosure and nameand-face disclosure conditions were significantly higher than in the anonymous condition, and contributions in the name-and-face disclosure condition were significantly higher than in the peer disclosure condition; proself individuals contributed significantly more in both disclosure conditions than in the anonymous condition, although their contributions did not differ significantly between the two disclosure conditions, and the gap between prosocial and proself individuals narrowed and was no longer significant in the name-and-face disclosure condition.

At the group level, the rate of sustained generations in both disclosure conditions was also significantly higher than in the anonymous condition, but it did not differ significantly between the peer disclosure and name-and-face disclosure conditions.

Taken together, when the audience consists of present peers, disclosing decisions can effectively increase intergenerational cooperation, and additionally disclosing names and faces was associated with a further increase.

In contrast to Experiment 1, in which disclosure to future generations did not significantly increase individual contributions, disclosure to present peers in this experiment significantly increased cooperation.
Beyond this, name-and-face disclosure was associated with further increases in intergenerational cooperation at the individual level.
However, this increase appeared only in individual token contributions and not in the rate of sustained generations.

This can be explained by a threshold account: In both conditions with disclosure to peers, participants' mean contributions were already above the fair share of 5 tokens per person, so most groups reached the contribution threshold anyway.

In this case, further increases in individual contributions mainly led groups that had already crossed the threshold to contribute more, rather than changing whether groups crossed it, and were therefore unlikely to produce a significant difference in a threshold-based group-level measure.
In addition, there were only slightly more than 40 groups per disclosure condition, so the group-level chi-square tests had relatively limited power.
Using the IGG as adapted by Lohse and Waichman (2020), the present research examined how two dimensions of reputational disclosure-audience and content-affect intergenerational cooperation.
text.formatted: Using the IGG as adapted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Lohse and Waichman (2020)</ref>, the present research examined how two dimensions of reputational disclosure-audience and content-affect intergenerational cooperation.

text.text: Disclosure to future generations increased the rate of sustained generations but did not significantly increase individual contributions or narrow the gap between prosocial and proself individuals, whereas disclosure to present peers increased both individual contributions and the rate of sustained generations.

Adding names and faces was associated with a further increase in contributions and, relative to the anonymous condition, with a significantly narrower prosocial-proself gap; in the name-and-face condition, the gap was no longer significant.
Taken together, the findings suggest that the two dimensions play different roles:

Whether the audience is present may determine whether disclosure reliably changes individual decisions, whereas the extent of identity disclosure may shape how strongly disclosure affects proself individuals.

Together, the results of the two experiments suggest that the mere act of disclosure may not be sufficient to promote intergenerational cooperation; its effect depends on the audience to whom the information is directed.
This dependence can be understood in terms of how reputation works.
In cooperation among contemporaries, reputation may help sustain cooperation through two routes.
The first is direct reciprocity, whereby, in repeated interactions, an individual's cooperation may be returned by the partner later on (Axelrod & Hamilton, 1981; Trivers, 1971).
text.formatted: The first is direct reciprocity, whereby, in repeated interactions, an individual's cooperation may be returned by the partner later on <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Axelrod & Hamilton, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Trivers, 1971)</ref>.

text.text: The second is indirect reciprocity, whereby cooperative behavior observed by third parties builds a good reputation, which in turn makes others more willing to cooperate with the individual in the future (Alexander, 1987; Nowak & Sigmund, 1998 , 2005).
text.formatted: The second is indirect reciprocity, whereby cooperative behavior observed by third parties builds a good reputation, which in turn makes others more willing to cooperate with the individual in the future <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alexander, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Nowak & Sigmund, 1998</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: In intergenerational contexts, the first route may be weakened: Because future generations cannot reciprocate toward the present generation, individuals' sacrifices are unlikely to be repaid through future returns.
More importantly, the payoff of the second route may also vary with the type of audience.

When information is disclosed to future generations, individuals can anticipate that they will have no further interaction or contact with them, so whatever reputation they build is unlikely to bring any real return.

When information is directed at peers, by contrast, individuals may expect some possibility of future interaction with this audience, so a good reputation is more likely to affect future opportunities for cooperation, which makes maintaining one's reputation an investment with potential returns.

Our results are consistent with this reasoning: Relative to the same anonymous baseline, disclosing decisions to contemporaries, with whom future interaction was possible, increased individual contributions, whereas disclosing the same decisions to future generations did not.
At the level of individual decisions, the audience that mattered was not the generation that would benefit from cooperation but the contemporaries who could observe the decision and respond to it.
This suggests that the prospect of future interaction may not be an incidental feature of the reputational mechanism but rather a prerequisite for it to work.

This interpretation is consistent with evidence that reputation sustains contributions to a public good only when later opportunities for indirect reciprocity are expected (Milinski et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2016) and that observability promotes prosociality more strongly when decisions can affect how others will later respond (Bradley et al., 2018), although reputational concerns can also restrain selfish behavior when no further economic interaction with the observer is expected (Arfer et al., 2015).

text.text: Moreover, the present research did not manipulate or measure participants' theory (Meyer et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Moreover, the present research did not manipulate or measure participants' theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Meyer et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: When situational cues are sufficiently explicit and the consequences of behavior are sufficiently clear, preexisting individual differences tend to explain less of the variation in behavior, and behavior is more likely to be governed by the external constraints and incentives provided by the situation.

In the present research, as the level of disclosure increased, proself individuals, who rely more on weighing external costs and benefits, were thus more likely to move toward the level of prosocial individuals and to behave more cooperatively (Simpson & Willer, 2008; Van Lange et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2016); meanwhile, prosocial individuals were already cooperating at a high level, so the gap between the two narrowed as disclosure increased.
text.formatted: In the present research, as the level of disclosure increased, proself individuals, who rely more on weighing external costs and benefits, were thus more likely to move toward the level of prosocial individuals and to behave more cooperatively <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Simpson & Willer, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Van Lange et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Wu et al., 2016)</ref>; meanwhile, prosocial individuals were already cooperating at a high level, so the gap between the two narrowed as disclosure increased.

text.text: This pattern fits the distinction proposed above: Disclosure, especially identifiable disclosure, appears to matter mainly for those who are least intrinsically motivated to cooperate.
For environmental psychology, the central implication is that making conservation visible on behalf of the future is not the same as making it accountable.

In our experiments, disclosure to the next generation was perceived as reputationally consequential but did little to change individual decisions, whereas the same information shown to present peers did.
This bears on how disclosure is designed in environmental governance.

Many instruments, such as carbon footprint labels, corporate sustainability reports, and intergenerational resource accounts, justify transparency by appeal to future generations, yet their behavioral force may depend on whether a contemporaneous audience (customers, investors, neighbors, or regulators) actually observes and evaluates what is disclosed.

Previous work has sustained intergenerational resources through binding median voting (Hauser et al., 2014) and partially improved their sustainability through costly peer punishment within a generation (Lohse & Waichman, 2020); our results suggest that a lower-cost lever, directing disclosure to a present audience and, where privacy and consent whether they crowd out intrinsic environmental motivation, or whether identifiable disclosure provokes reactance and privacy concerns are questions the present data cannot answer but that any intervention recommendation must eventually confront.

text.text: More broadly, the difficulty with disclosure to future generations lies less in their relevance than in their absence-and that absence is a design problem for institutions, not only for experiments.
Intergenerational environmental dilemmas pose a distinctive problem for reputationbased cooperation: the people who benefit from present restraint are not yet there to see it.
Across two experiments, we found that disclosure promoted intergenerational cooperation, but its strength depended on who received the information and what the information revealed.
Disclosing contributions to the next generation helped more groups pass the resource on but did not reliably change individual decisions.

Disclosing the same contributions to present peers raised individual contributions as well, and adding names and faces was associated with a further increase, concentrated among proself individuals, to the point that their contributions no longer differed significantly from those of prosocial individuals.
Our results refine the view that reputation sustains cooperation.

In intergenerational settings, visibility appears to translate into restraint chiefly when an audience is present to observe and evaluate the decision, and disclosure, especially identifiable disclosure, appears to matter most for those least motivated to cooperate.
For environmental communication and disclosure policy, the implication is that transparency directed at posterity is a weak lever on its own.
It is more likely to change behavior when paired with contemporaneous accountability and, within the limits of privacy and consent, when those whose decisions affect the future can be identified.
Whether these principles hold beyond the laboratory remains to be established.

The next steps are to separate audience presence from the anticipated interaction that accompanies it, to replicate the identity effect in a fully randomized design, and to test disclosure in real environmental decisions with more diverse populations.

A particularly promising direction is to give future generations a present voice, through proxies or institutional representatives who can observe and evaluate today's decisions on their behalf, and to ask whether doing so restores the reputational force that distant audiences lack.
Evidence that taking the perspective of future generations before deciding reduces unsustainable choices (Shahen et al., 2021) makes this direction worth pursuing.

text.text: Given that disclosing decisions to peers does promote intergenerational cooperation, the question that follows is how this effect can be further enhanced.

Disclosing decisions alone conveys behavioral information without revealing the actor's identity, whereas adding names and faces links the behavior to a specific, identifiable individual (Bradley et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Disclosing decisions alone conveys behavioral information without revealing the actor's identity, whereas adding names and faces links the behavior to a specific, identifiable individual <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bradley et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: We found that disclosing names and faces in addition to decisions was associated with higher token contributions, in line with previous findings that identifiability promotes cooperation (Christens et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2017) and that information about others' identities matters mainly when it accompanies information about their behavior (Sampaio et al., 2023).
text.formatted: We found that disclosing names and faces in addition to decisions was associated with higher token contributions, in line with previous findings that identifiability promotes cooperation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Christens et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Wang et al., 2017)</ref> and that information about others' identities matters mainly when it accompanies information about their behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Sampaio et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A meta-analysis, however, found no reliable difference between manipulations that reveal both identity and behavior and those that reveal behavior alone (Bradley et al., 2018), so this additional benefit should be interpreted with caution, particularly because the name-and-face condition was recruited in a separate wave.
text.formatted: A meta-analysis, however, found no reliable difference between manipulations that reveal both identity and behavior and those that reveal behavior alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bradley et al., 2018)</ref>, so this additional benefit should be interpreted with caution, particularly because the name-and-face condition was recruited in a separate wave.

text.text: More notably, this increase was not equal across individuals.

Prosocial individuals' contributions remained high in all conditions and did not change significantly with disclosure condition, whereas proself individuals contributed significantly more in both disclosure conditions than in the anonymous condition.
The gap between the two was significantly narrower under name-and-face disclosure than in the anonymous condition and was no longer significant in that condition.

Among proself individuals, strategy changes were concentrated at the two ends: The proportion of free riders decreased and the proportion of supercooperators increased, whereas the proportion of precise cooperators remained largely unchanged.
For prosocial individuals, the proportions of precise cooperation and supercooperation did not differ significantly across the three conditions.
These results are consistent with situational strength allow, making actors identifiable, may achieve part of the same effect.

Practical measures should not stop at disclosure as a formality; they also need to ensure that the disclosed information reaches a present audience that is able to observe and evaluate the behavior, so that reputational pressure can actually take effect.

At the same time, provided that regulatory requirements are met and privacy consent is obtained, the identifiability of the information and the extent to which behavior can be attributed to individuals should be moderately increased.
Because this effect of disclosure was more pronounced among proself individuals, such interventions may also help, to some extent, narrow differences in cooperation within groups.
Several questions remain open, not as oversights of the present design but as extensions that the design itself was not built to settle.
The first concerns what audience presence means in our design.

Because future-generation and peer disclosure were tested against a shared anonymous baseline, the contrast between them is indirect, and the two audiences differed in more than their presence at the time of decision: peers were co-actors who faced the same choice, whose own contributions were also disclosed, and with whom participants might have expected further contact, whereas the next generation consisted of recipients whom participants had no reason to expect to meet.

Presence in our design is therefore a bundle of featurestemporal co-location, mutual exposure, and the prospect of future interaction-and we cannot say which of them carries the effect; a crossed design that varies these features independently, for example by disclosing decisions to peers who will never be met again, would turn this interpretation into a test.

A second limitation concerns the sample: given the constraints, participants were recruited in two waves and had an uneven age and gender composition, and a broader sample is needed to test the boundaries of these conclusions.
Finally, we measured only immediate behavior: whether reputation-driven contributions persist once observation ends,

The research comprised two experiments.

Experiment 1 focused on disclosing the decisions of members of the current generation to future generations and examined whether reputational pressure in an intergenerational context can increase the intergenerational cooperation of proself individuals.

Experiment 2 replaced the audience with members of the current generation and manipulated the type of information disclosed to test whether disclosing decisions to peers promotes intergenerational cooperation more effectively; it further tested whether, as more information is disclosed, the intergenerational cooperation of proself individuals comes closer to that of prosocial individuals.

By examining who can observe conservation-relevant decisions and what identity information is disclosed, the present research investigates when reputational concerns may help sustain cooperation across generations, offering insight into the psychological processes that can support conservation for future generations.

Experiment 1 first tested whether, compared with the anonymous condition, future-generation decision disclosure increases the intergenerational cooperation of members of the current generation.

Second, because SVO may affect individuals' sensitivity to reputational cues, Experiment 1 compared the intergenerational cooperation of prosocial and proself individuals in the two conditions to examine whether future-generation decision disclosure narrows the gap in intergenerational cooperation between individuals with different SVOs.
